15450:
Vague means not clear, not specific, and not precise enough to be fully understood or pinned down.

Think of it this way. Imagine you are looking at something through a foggy window. You can tell something is there, but you cannot make out its exact shape, color, or details. That foggy, blurry quality — that is what "vague" captures. It describes anything that is fuzzy, uncertain, or lacking sharpness, whether we are talking about words, ideas, shapes, memories, or even feelings.

"Vague" is a flexible word. It can describe many different kinds of things. Here are the main ones:

1. Language and communication

This is the most common use. When someone says something vague, their words do not give you enough information to truly understand what they mean.

  • "He gave me a vague answer."

He said something, yes — but after hearing it, you still do not know exactly what he meant. He was not specific.

  • "The instructions were vague."

The instructions existed, but they were not detailed or clear enough for you to follow them confidently.

  • "She made a vague promise to help."

She said she would help, but she gave no details — no time, no plan, no commitment. It was fuzzy and uncertain.

2. Ideas and thoughts

Sometimes a thought or plan has not taken a solid, clear shape in someone's mind yet. It exists, but only loosely.

  • "I have a vague idea of what I want to do with my life."

There is some direction, but it is not formed into a concrete, clear plan yet.

  • "He had a vague sense that something was wrong."

He felt uneasy, but he could not point to exactly what was causing that feeling or why.

3. Shapes and appearance

Vague can also describe something you see that does not have a sharp, clear outline — something blurry or hard to define visually.

  • "Through the fog, I could see the vague outline of a building."

The building was there, but its edges and details were blurred and unclear.

4. Memories

When a memory is vague, you remember that something happened, but the details are blurry and incomplete.

  • "I have a vague memory of meeting her as a child."

You are not sure of the exact details — maybe just a face, or a feeling, but nothing sharp or complete.

5. A person's behavior

When a person is described as being vague, it means they are not being clear, detailed, or direct in what they say or do.

  • "She was very vague when I asked her where she had been."

She answered, perhaps, but her answer left a lot of questions unanswered. She did not give you the full picture.
The Key Quality: A Lack of Sharpness

The thread connecting all these uses is a single idea: something is there, but it is not sharp or clear enough to fully grasp. Vague things exist in a kind of in-between zone — not absent, but not fully present either. Not zero information, but not enough information.

This is important. Vague is not the same as wrong or false or nothing. It simply means the edges are blurry. There is substance, but the details are missing.

Vagueness can happen in two ways, and understanding this distinction makes the word richer.

Unintentional vagueness happens when someone is genuinely unclear because they do not know enough, have not thought it through, or simply cannot express themselves precisely.

  • "The scientist gave a vague explanation because the research was still incomplete."

Intentional vagueness happens when someone chooses to be unclear — often to avoid commitment, hide something, or dodge a difficult question.

  • "The politician gave deliberately vague answers so he could not be held to anything."

In this second case, "vague" often carries a slightly negative tone, suggesting someone is being evasive or dishonest by not saying what they really mean.

Something can be slightly vague or extremely vague. The word works on a scale.

  • A slightly vague answer might be 80% clear but missing one or two key details.
  • An extremely vague answer might give you almost nothing useful at all.

You will often see it paired with words that show degree:

  • "The directions were a little vague." — somewhat unclear
  • "The directions were incredibly vague." — almost useless, very unclear
  • "The directions were rather vague." — noticeably unclear

Understanding how "vague" compares to related words sharpens your understanding of it.

  • Unclear — a broad, general word for something that is not easy to understand. Vague and unclear often overlap, but unclear can also describe something that is difficult to understand for other reasons (like being too complicated), while vague specifically points to a lack of detail and precision.
  • Ambiguous — something ambiguous has two or more possible meanings, and you cannot tell which one is intended. Vague means there is not enough information; ambiguous means there is just enough information to confuse you in two different directions. "His vague response gave me nothing to work with. His ambiguous response could have meant two completely opposite things."
  • Hazy — very similar to vague, often used for memories, thoughts, or visual things. It has a slightly more poetic or sensory feeling to it. "My memory of that day is hazy" feels slightly softer and more atmospheric than "My memory of that day is vague," but the meaning is nearly the same.
  • Fuzzy — informal and very similar to vague or hazy. Often used in casual speech for memories and thinking. "The details are a bit fuzzy."
  • Indefinite — means not fixed, not clearly decided, or without a defined limit. "We leave on an indefinite date" means no specific date has been set. It overlaps with vague but is used more for things like plans, time, and quantities.
  • Nebulous — a more formal, academic-sounding word that means almost exactly what vague means, but with an extra sense of something being cloud-like and shapeless. "A nebulous concept" is one that has no firm form at all.

Knowing the opposite of a word is one of the best ways to understand it deeply.

The opposites of vague include:

  • Clear — easily understood, well-expressed
  • Precise — exactly right, with no unnecessary looseness
  • Specific — naming or describing something in exact, concrete detail
  • Definite — firmly decided, certain, not open to doubt
  • Explicit — fully and clearly stated, leaving nothing to the imagination

"Can you give me a more specific answer?" is essentially the same as saying "Can you stop being so vague?"

In real English, "vague" most often appears in these combinations:

  • a vague answer / response / reply — when someone does not say enough
  • a vague memory / recollection — a fuzzy, incomplete memory
  • a vague idea / notion / sense / feeling — something not yet fully formed in the mind
  • a vague outline / shape / figure — something seen without sharp edges
  • a vague promise / commitment — a promise without real detail or firmness
  • vague instructions / directions — guidance that is not clear enough to follow
  • deliberately / intentionally vague — when someone chooses to be unclear on purpose
  • rather / somewhat / a bit vague — moderately unclear
  • remain vague — to continue to be unclear without offering more detail
One Final Way to Remember It

If you ever forget what vague means, picture a foggy morning. You can see the world around you — the trees, the buildings, the road — but nothing has sharp edges. Everything exists, but nothing is fully clear. That fog is vagueness. When the sun rises and burns the fog away, everything becomes specific, clear, and precise — the opposite of vague.

That image captures the word perfectly.
15451: "Vain" has two distinct meanings, and both are very common in English. You need to know both to truly own this word.
Meaning 1 — Excessively proud of yourself, especially your looks

This is the meaning most people think of first. A vain person is someone who thinks too highly of themselves — particularly about how they look, how talented they are, or how important they are. It goes beyond normal confidence. A vain person is obsessed with their own image and craves the admiration of others.

The important nuance is that vanity is hollow pride — it's self-admiration that isn't earned or that isn't backed by real depth of character. A vain person isn't just proud; they are excessively and shallowly self-focused.

Think of it this way: Imagine someone who checks their reflection in every mirror and shop window they pass, constantly fishes for compliments, gets genuinely upset if no one notices their new haircut, and somehow makes every conversation about themselves. That's vain.

Examples in sentences:

  • "She was so vain that she brought a pocket mirror to dinner."
  • "He was too vain to admit he was wrong — it would have damaged his image."
  • "Don't be so vain; the world doesn't revolve around how you look."

The noun form of this meaning is vanity — as in, "His vanity made him impossible to work with." You may also know the word vainglorious, which means essentially the same thing but stronger and more literary — boastfully proud and self-congratulatory.
Meaning 2 — Producing no result; pointless; unsuccessful

This second meaning is completely different from the first, but equally important. When an effort, attempt, or action is described as vain, it means it achieved nothing. It failed. It was wasted. No matter how hard someone tried, the result was zero.

Examples:

  • "The rescue team made a vain attempt to reach the survivors before the storm hit."
  • "All his hard work was vain — the project was cancelled anyway."
  • "She made a vain effort to stay awake during the lecture."

The phrase "in vain" is one of the most important expressions built from this meaning, and you will encounter it constantly. It simply means without success or for nothing.

  • "She tried in vain to open the jar." — She tried but failed.
  • "He waited for hours, but it was all in vain — she never showed up."
  • "They searched in vain for the missing keys."

Whenever you see or hear "in vain," you can reliably substitute the words "without success" and the sentence will mean the same thing.
The phrase "take someone's name in vain"

You will almost certainly encounter this phrase, especially in religious or formal contexts. To take someone's name in vain means to use a person's name — most often God's name — carelessly, disrespectfully, or without any real purpose. It treats a name that deserves reverence as if it were trivial or meaningless.

  • "The commandment says not to take the Lord's name in vain."

In everyday modern use, it's also used informally and sometimes humorously to mean mentioning someone's name without good reason:

  • "Were you taking my name in vain while I was out of the room?" (= Were you talking about me behind my back?)
Why do these two meanings belong to the same word?

At first glance, "too proud" and "useless/unsuccessful" seem completely unrelated. But there is a deep connecting thread: emptiness beneath the surface.

A vain person's pride is empty — it's not rooted in real character or real achievement. A vain effort is empty too — it looked like it was going somewhere but ultimately produced nothing. Both meanings circle around the idea of something that appears to have substance or value but is, underneath, hollow.
Don't confuse it with its homophones

"Vain," "vane," and "vein" are all pronounced identically, but they are completely different words:

  • Vain (adjective) — what you just learned.
  • Vane (noun) — a flat blade that rotates in the wind, like a weather vane on top of a barn.
  • Vein (noun) — the vessels that carry blood through your body, or a streak of mineral running through rock (a vein of gold, for example).

When writing, always ask yourself: am I talking about a personality trait or a failed effort (vain), something that spins in wind (vane), or something in a body or rock (vein)?

Vain as an adjective means one of two things:

1. A person who is too focused on and proud of their own appearance, talents, or status — hollow, self-absorbed pride.

2. An effort or attempt that is useless and produces no result — pointless, unsuccessful, wasted.

And in the fixed phrase "in vain" = without success.
15452:
Vainglorious describes a person who is excessively proud of their own achievements or abilities — and, crucially, cannot stop showing it off. It's not just about thinking highly of yourself privately. A vainglorious person performs their pride. They want an audience. They want to be admired, praised, and recognized — and they actively work to make that happen by boasting, showing off, or drawing constant attention to their own greatness.

Think of it as two things happening at once: an inflated sense of self-importance, and a compulsive need to put that importance on display for the world.

The word "vain" in vainglorious carries a particular shade of meaning. It doesn't just mean proud — it means emptily or excessively proud. Often, the glory a vainglorious person seeks is either undeserved, grossly exaggerated, or simply not as impressive as they make it out to be. There's a hollowness to it. They are chasing admiration the way someone might chase a shadow — loudly, urgently, and without real substance to back it up.

Even when their achievements are real, the vainglorious person magnifies them far beyond what is reasonable or dignified.
The "glory" part — what they're actually after

The glory in vainglorious tells you what they want: fame, honor, recognition, applause. They are not just proud in a quiet, internal way. They want the whole room to know. They want their name remembered. They want credit — loudly, publicly, repeatedly.

A vainglorious general, for example, doesn't just win a battle and move on. He makes sure every soldier, every citizen, every historian knows he won it, how brilliantly he won it, and exactly how inferior everyone else would have been in his place.
How it's different from similar words

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Proud is neutral or even positive. A mother is proud of her daughter. A craftsman is proud of his work. Nothing wrong there. Vainglorious is never positive — it is always a criticism.

Arrogant people look downward — they think others are beneath them. Vainglorious people look outward — they are obsessed with how they appear and what they are getting in return (praise, status, admiration). An arrogant person dismisses others. A vainglorious person just can't stop talking about themselves.

Conceited is close — it means having an unreasonably high opinion of yourself. But conceit can be internal and quiet. Vaingloriousness is always outward and theatrical. A conceited person thinks they're great. A vainglorious person announces it.

Boastful is the closest everyday synonym — it means someone who brags. Vainglorious includes boastfulness, but it's richer and more complete. It captures not just the bragging, but the entire posture of self-glorification: the self-promotion, the hunger for admiration, and the exaggerated sense of one's own importance. Vainglorious is the full picture; boastful is just one piece of it.
The tone and register of this word

Vainglorious is a formal, literary word. You're unlikely to hear it in casual conversation. You're more likely to encounter it in books, historical writing, biographies, journalism, or thoughtful criticism. When someone uses it, they are delivering a precise, sharp, and rather unflattering judgment about a person's character.

It always has a negative connotation. There is no kind way to call someone vainglorious. It is a criticism, through and through.
Real-world examples to make it stick

Imagine a politician who, in every single speech, references his own past decisions, achievements, and sacrifices — even when the topic has nothing to do with him. He can't resist reminding everyone how much he has done and how uniquely capable he is. That's vainglorious.

Imagine a businessman who paid for a giant portrait of himself to hang in his company's lobby, who name-drops his own wealth constantly, and who responds to every team success by steering the credit toward himself. Vainglorious.

Imagine a historical king who built enormous statues of himself across the kingdom, commissioned poets to write about his battles, and insisted on being called "The Great" long before anyone else agreed he deserved the title. Classically vainglorious.
How to use it in a sentence

• "The vainglorious CEO couldn't give an interview without boasting about his net worth."
  • "His vainglorious speeches, full of self-congratulation, made even his supporters cringe."
  • "She was brilliant, but her vainglorious attitude made it impossible for others to give her genuine praise — she had already given it all to herself."

A vainglorious person is someone who is excessively, theatrically, and publicly proud of themselves — who hunts for admiration, brags about their own achievements (often beyond what is warranted), and seems incapable of letting the world forget how great they believe themselves to be.
15453:
Vainglory is an excessive, hollow pride in yourself and your achievements, combined with a burning desire to show that pride off and be admired for it by others.

Notice there are two things happening at once:

  • An inflated, over-the-top sense of your own greatness
  • A deep craving for praise, recognition, and fame from other people

Neither part alone is the full picture. Vainglory is both together. It is the feeling of "I am magnificent" and the hunger for the whole world to notice and applaud.

The word vain carries a specific weight. When we say something is vain, we mean it is empty, hollow, and without real substance. The glory that a vainglorious person seeks is vain glory — a kind of fame or admiration that has no solid foundation. It is not glory earned through genuine greatness or deep virtue. It is glory craved for its own sake, often built on exaggeration, boasting, or superficiality.

Think of it this way: a truly great person might feel pride in their work. That pride is grounded. But a vainglorious person either exaggerates modest achievements into towering ones, or hungers for praise so desperately that the praise itself becomes more important than the actual achievement. The glory is the point, not a byproduct.

To understand vainglory deeply, picture this internal monologue:

"I need people to see how great I am. I need to be praised, celebrated, and looked up to. My achievements — real or embellished — must be on full display at all times. Being great is not enough. I must be seen as great."

A vainglorious person is not merely confident. They are addicted to admiration. There is a restlessness to it — a constant need to perform, to boast, to be recognised. If no one is watching, no one is praising, no one is impressed, the vainglorious person feels empty. The self-worth here is entirely borrowed from other people's opinions.

This is also why vainglory is considered a flaw, not just a personality trait. It means your ego is so fragile and hungry that you cannot simply do good work and be at peace. You must have the spotlight. You must have the applause.
How It Shows Up in Real Life

• A colleague who constantly reminds everyone of their past successes, even in conversations where it has no relevance.
  • A leader who makes decisions not based on what is best, but on what will make them look most impressive.
  • A person who does a kind act — donates to charity, helps someone — but only if other people will hear about it and praise them for it. If it had to be done in secret, they would lose interest.
  • Someone who exaggerates the difficulty of their work so others will be more impressed by it.
  • A person who cannot tolerate being second-best, not because they have high standards, but because being second means someone else gets more admiration.
How It Is Different From Similar Words

These words are close neighbours but are not the same:

Pride can be healthy. You can feel proud of genuine hard work, and that pride can motivate you. Vainglory is pride that has gone rotten — it is excessive, often undeserved, and entirely dependent on an audience.

Arrogance means you look down on others and believe you are superior to them. It is about hierarchy. Vainglory is less about putting others below you and more about pulling admiration toward you. An arrogant person may not even care if you notice them — they already know they're superior. A vainglorious person desperately needs you to notice.

Vanity is often about appearance and self-image — obsessing over how you look, how you come across, how polished your image is. Vainglory is specifically about glory — fame, honour, praise, and recognition for your achievements or greatness, not just your looks.

Boastfulness is the behaviour — the act of bragging. Vainglory is the underlying condition — the deep character trait or state of mind that makes a person boastful. Boastfulness is a symptom; vainglory is the disease.

Vainglory is a formal and literary word. You will encounter it more in classic literature, philosophy, religious writing, and serious essays than in everyday conversation. In everyday speech, people might instead say someone is "full of themselves," "a show-off," or "always bragging." But vainglory captures all of that in one precise word, with an extra layer of meaning — the hollowness and hunger for praise — that those casual phrases do not fully capture.

When you see this word, it is almost always used critically, to describe a character flaw. Nobody calls someone vainglorious as a compliment.

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: Vainglory is an excessive, hollow pride paired with an obsessive craving for admiration and praise from others — a hunger to be seen as great, rather than to actually be great.
15454:
A valance is a short, decorative strip of fabric — or sometimes wood or metal — that is attached along the top edge of something (usually a window or a bed) to make it look neat and attractive, and to hide things that aren't meant to be seen, like rods, rails, or frames.

Think of it as a "decorative cover-up." Its job is equal parts beauty and concealment.
The Two Main Places You'll Find a Valance

1. On a Window

When you hang curtains on a window, there's usually a metal or plastic rod at the very top holding them up. That rod, along with its brackets and hooks, is functional but ugly. A window valance is a short, horizontal strip of fabric hung across the very top of the window — in front of the rod — to hide all of that hardware from view.

Unlike full curtains, a window valance does not run the full length of the window. It only covers the top portion — usually about 12 to 18 inches deep — and stays in place permanently. The actual curtains (if any) hang below it and can be opened or closed. The valance just sits there, framing the top of the window and giving it a finished, polished look.

It can be plain and flat, or it can be ruffled, pleated, draped, or shaped — depending on the style of the room.

2. On a Bed

A bed has several layers: a mattress on top, a box spring (a rigid support base) beneath it, and a bed frame holding everything up. The box spring and frame are purely structural — again, functional but unattractive.

A bed valance (also commonly called a bed skirt) is a piece of fabric that sits between the mattress and the box spring, with its edges hanging down on three sides of the bed (the two long sides and the foot-end), all the way to the floor. This creates the appearance of a "skirt" around the lower part of the bed, hiding the box spring, the metal frame, and whatever might be stored underneath the bed.
What Makes a Valance Different from a Curtain?

This is an important distinction:

  • A curtain hangs the full length of a window, moves (you open and close it), and its main purpose is to control light and privacy.
  • A valance is short, stationary, and its main purpose is decoration and concealment.

You can have a valance without curtains beneath it (just to decorate a window), or you can have a valance with curtains (where the valance hides the top hardware and the curtains do the actual work below).
What It Can Be Made Of

While fabric is by far the most common material, a valance can also be made of:

  • Wood — shaped and painted or stained, often seen in kitchens or in very structured, formal window designs. These are sometimes called cornices or pelmet boards, though the term valance is often used loosely for these too.
  • Metal — sometimes used in modern or industrial interior design.
  • Fabric variations — cotton, linen, silk, velvet, or synthetic blends, depending on the room's style.
The One Word That Captures It

If you had to sum up a valance in one word, that word would be: "topper."

It tops a window. It tops a bed. It hides what's beneath it and makes the whole thing look intentional and complete. That's a valance.

Imagine a stage in a theatre. Above the stage, there's a horizontal strip of curtain running across the very top — hiding the lights, ropes, and rigging above. The audience only sees a clean, decorative border framing the top of the stage. That horizontal strip? In theatre, it's called a "valance" or "pelmet" for the same reason — it conceals the mechanics and adds beauty.

That image maps perfectly onto how a valance works in your home.
15455:
A vale is a valley — a low-lying stretch of land that sits between hills or areas of higher ground, usually with a river or stream running gently through it.

That's the heart of it. But there's much more texture to this word worth knowing.

Not all valleys are the same, and "vale" has a particular feel to it. When you picture a vale, picture something wide, open, and gently sheltered — not a dramatic rocky gorge or a tight narrow ravine, but a soft, broad, peaceful piece of lowland, cradled on either side by rolling hills. Think green meadows, a quiet river winding through the middle, maybe some scattered trees. It's a calm, almost gentle kind of landscape.

A vale is not steep, dramatic, or dangerous-looking. It's pastoral. Quiet. Settled.
It's a Literary and Poetic Word

This is crucial: in modern, everyday conversation, almost nobody says "vale." If you're describing a valley to a friend, you'd say valley. "Vale" belongs to poetry, literature, hymns, and formal writing. It has an old-fashioned, elevated, almost romantic quality to it.

You'll encounter it in:

  • Classic poetry and literature (Shakespeare used it, for example)
  • Hymns and religious texts
  • Place names (more on that below)
  • Formal or deliberately elevated prose

So if you read "vale" in a novel or poem, you know the writer is being deliberately lyrical or old-fashioned in tone.

One of the most common places you'll still see "vale" today is in geographical place names, particularly in Britain:

  • Vale of Evesham — a famous fertile farming valley in England
  • Vale of Kashmir — the renowned valley in India
  • Vale of Glamorgan — a region in Wales
  • Tunbridge Wells sits near a vale

In this context, "vale" simply names the valley as a geographical area — it's used as a proper noun. You'll notice it's typically written as "Vale of [place name]," which is a classic structure.

These are fixed expressions using "vale" that you're very likely to encounter:

1. "Vale of tears"

This is the most famous and widely used phrase. It refers to life on Earth, viewed as a place of suffering, hardship, and sorrow. It comes from a long religious and literary tradition that saw earthly life as painful and fleeting — a "vale" (a low, earthly place) filled with "tears" (human suffering).

"She endured this vale of tears with quiet dignity."

Even today, this phrase is used — sometimes solemnly, sometimes ironically — to describe the struggles of life.

2. "The vale of years"

This phrase refers to old age — the later, declining years of a person's life. Shakespeare used it in Othello. Just as a vale is the lower ground at the end of a journey through hills, "the vale of years" is the final, downward slope of a human life.

"He had reached the vale of years, but his mind remained sharp."
How It Compares to Similar Words

English has several words for valley-like landscapes, and it helps to know where "vale" fits:

  • Valley — the everyday, neutral, modern word. Use this in normal conversation.
  • Vale — poetic, literary, old-fashioned. Same basic meaning, but elevated in tone.
  • Dale — also poetic, mostly used in northern England (think the Yorkshire Dales). A dale is often narrower and more rugged than a vale.
  • Glen — a Scottish and Irish word for a narrow mountain valley.
  • Dell — a small, secluded, wooded hollow or valley. Smaller and more enclosed than a vale.

Among these, vale is the broadest and most open, and the most consciously "literary" in feel.

If you saw the sentence:

"The shepherd led his flock down into the misty vale as evening fell,"

you would know: the shepherd is descending into a wide, quiet, low-lying valley. The word "vale" here also gives the sentence a gentle, poetic atmosphere — it makes the scene feel timeless and a little romantic.

And if you saw:

"She said life is nothing but a vale of tears,"

you would know: she means that life is full of suffering and hardship — she's using the classic idiom, not literally describing a landscape.
Vale (noun) = a valley, especially a wide and gentle one; used mainly in poetry, literature, place names, and fixed phrases like "vale of tears" (meaning a life of suffering).
15456: A valediction is a farewell — but not just any casual goodbye. It is the formal, deliberate, often deeply felt act of saying goodbye, or the actual words spoken or written to do so. When something meaningful comes to an end — a career, a school chapter, a leader's final term in office — and someone marks that ending with carefully chosen words of farewell, those words are a valediction.

Valediction has two closely related but distinct uses, and knowing both gives you the full picture.

The first and broader meaning is a farewell speech or statement — any formal, meaningful goodbye that acknowledges something is truly ending. At a graduation ceremony, the top student stands before their classmates and delivers a farewell address: that speech is a valediction. When a president, CEO, or ambassador gives their final public address before leaving their post, that address is their valediction. When a beloved teacher speaks to students on their last day, sending them off into the world — that, too, is a valediction. Notice the common thread: these are not casual goodbyes. A valediction marks a real, significant ending.

The second meaning is more specific and belongs to the world of formal writing. In a letter or email, a valediction is the short closing phrase you write just before signing your name — the written equivalent of a goodbye. "Yours sincerely," "Kind regards," "With love," and "Best wishes" are all valedictions. They are the brief, conventional farewell phrases that close a piece of correspondence.
The Character and Tone of a Valediction

A valediction always carries a certain gravity. It is formal or ceremonial by nature — you would never use the word to describe a quick wave to a friend on the street. It signals something truly ending, not a temporary parting. And it is deliberate: the person giving a valediction chooses their words with intention and care. This is not an offhand goodbye; it is a composed and considered one.

"The retiring professor gave a heartfelt valediction to his students before leaving the university for the last time." — here, the valediction is his farewell speech.

"Her valediction at the end of the ceremony moved the entire audience to tears." — again, the farewell address itself.

"'Yours faithfully' is a traditional valediction used in formal business letters." — here, the valediction is the closing phrase of a letter.

"The soldier's final letter home ended with a tender valediction that his family kept forever." — the closing phrase, something like "With all my love."

"The departing mayor delivered her valediction to a packed city hall." — a farewell speech marking the end of her tenure.

Two words from the same family are worth learning alongside this one.

A valedictorian is the student — typically the one with the highest academic standing in their class — who is chosen to deliver the valediction (the farewell speech) at a graduation ceremony. The word is essentially built around the concept: the valedictorian is the one who gives the valediction.

Valedictory is the adjective form. You might hear of a "valedictory address," a "valedictory speech," or a "valedictory gesture" — all of which simply mean something that relates to, or expresses, a farewell.

A valediction, then, is the language of farewell — whether that means a moving speech at the end of a long career, a graduation address that closes a chapter of school life, or the quiet "Kind regards" at the bottom of a business letter. What unites every use of the word is the same core idea: someone is marking an ending with words. The context is formal, the occasion carries meaning, and the goodbye is meant to be felt — not just said.
15457:
A valedictorian is the student who graduates with the highest academic rank in their entire class. That's the heart of it. If you and 500 other students graduate from a high school or college together, and you have the best academic record among all 500 of you, you are the valedictorian of that graduating class.

The title is awarded once per graduating class. It belongs to exactly one person — the top student.
How Does Someone Become a Valedictorian?

Academic rank is almost always determined by GPA (Grade Point Average) — a number that represents the average of all a student's grades across all their courses throughout their time at that school. The student with the highest GPA at the time of graduation earns the title.

Because even a single low grade can affect the GPA, valedictorians are typically students who have worked consistently hard across every subject, every semester, for their entire time at that school — not just in one impressive final year.
The Main Duty: The Valedictory Speech

Being named valedictorian comes with an important honor and responsibility: the valedictorian traditionally delivers the farewell speech at the graduation ceremony (also called the commencement ceremony).

This speech is called the valedictory address. It is addressed to the graduating class and is meant to be a meaningful send-off — often reflecting on shared experiences, offering encouragement, and looking ahead to the future. It is usually the most prominent student speech of the entire ceremony, and it is a significant public honor to be the one giving it.
Where and When Is This Title Used?

The term is most commonly used in the United States, and it applies at both the high school and college/university level. Every graduating class — whether a small class of 30 students or a large university class of thousands — can have its own valedictorian.

The title is only relevant at the moment of graduation. It does not follow a person throughout life as an ongoing credential, but it is considered a prestigious achievement that people often mention in resumes, college applications, and biographical summaries.

You will often hear the word "valedictorian" alongside another word: salutatorian. The salutatorian is the student with the second-highest academic rank in the graduating class. The salutatorian also typically gives a speech at graduation, but it comes before the valedictorian's speech and is generally considered the secondary honor. Think of valedictorian as the gold medal and salutatorian as the silver medal.

Sometimes, two or more students finish with identical GPAs — so high that no single student stands clearly above the rest. In these cases, many schools choose to name co-valedictorians, sharing the title among all students who are tied at the top. This has become more common over time, particularly as grading practices have evolved and more students achieve perfect or near-perfect GPAs.

Some people feel co-valedictorians is a fair solution; others feel it dilutes the meaning of the title. Schools handle this differently.
A Growing Debate: Should the Title Exist at All?

In recent decades, some schools and education experts have questioned whether the valedictorian system is healthy. Their concern is that the intense competition for the top GPA can push students to make choices driven purely by grades — such as avoiding challenging courses that might lower their GPA — rather than pursuing genuine learning and intellectual curiosity.

As a result, some schools have abolished the valedictorian title entirely, choosing instead to honor all students who meet a high academic standard (a practice sometimes called "Latin honors," where graduates are recognized as cum laude, magna cum laude, or summa cum laude depending on their GPA range). Other schools have kept the tradition, seeing it as a meaningful way to recognize the highest achiever.

To remember this word simply: a valedictorian is the #1 student in a graduating class, who gives the farewell speech at graduation. Every part of the word's meaning connects to those two things — the achievement of being the best academically, and the honor of being the one who formally says goodbye to the class on everyone's behalf.
15458:
If something is valedictory, it is related to, or has the character of, a farewell — specifically a formal, intentional, and often emotionally significant goodbye that marks the end of something important.

The key idea is not just that something is last or final, but that it consciously acknowledges its own ending. It carries a sense of looking back, wrapping up, and departing with purpose.

Think about the last day of school before graduation, or a retiring athlete's final game, or a president's last speech before leaving office. There's a particular atmosphere to those moments — reflective, a little solemn, tinged with both pride and bittersweetness. That atmosphere is exactly what "valedictory" captures.

It is not just any ending. It is an ending that knows it is an ending and acknowledges that openly, often with a sense of ceremony or dignity.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Valedictory?

The adjective can describe a wide range of things, as long as they carry that farewell quality:

  • A valedictory speech — a formal farewell address, given before someone departs a role, an institution, or a stage of life. The most classic example is a graduation speech. A retiring CEO might give a valedictory address to their company.
  • A valedictory performance — a musician, actor, or athlete's final show or game, treated as a send-off. A band performing their last-ever concert could be called a valedictory performance.
  • A valedictory letter or message — a written farewell, often carrying reflection and a sense of closure. A diplomat writing a final dispatch before leaving their post might write a valedictory letter.
  • A valedictory tour — a final tour undertaken specifically to say goodbye. A retiring comedian doing a last run of shows across the country is on a valedictory tour.
  • A valedictory gesture — a final act that signals goodbye or serves as a parting statement. A leader's last major policy decision before stepping down could be called a valedictory gesture.
  • A valedictory mood or tone — even an atmosphere or feeling can be valedictory. If a novel's final chapter feels reflective, wistful, and closing, you could say it has a valedictory tone.

• "The veteran journalist wrote a valedictory column after 40 years at the newspaper, reflecting on everything she had witnessed."
  • "His valedictory speech moved the audience to tears — it felt like the closing of an era."
  • "The team's last match of the season, knowing they were losing their star player, had a valedictory quality to it."
  • "She sent a valedictory email to her colleagues on her final day at the company."
What Makes It Different From Similar Words?

This is important for precision.

  • "Final" simply means last in a sequence. A final exam is just the last exam. It has no emotional farewell quality built into it.
  • "Last" works the same way — purely positional. The last train is just the train after which no more come.
  • "Farewell" (as an adjective, e.g., "a farewell party") is the closest everyday equivalent, but it is more casual and general. "Valedictory" is more formal, more elevated, and carries a stronger suggestion of significance, reflection, and ceremony.
  • "Elegiac" means mournful or expressing grief about a loss, and while it can overlap in feeling, it leans more toward sadness about something already gone. Valedictory is about the act of departing, not purely the mourning of it.

So "valedictory" sits at the intersection of formal, farewell, and reflective. It's the word you reach for when a goodbye is significant enough to deserve acknowledgment and ceremony.

This is a formal and literary word. You will encounter it in:

  • Journalism and opinion writing ("his valedictory address to the nation")
  • Literary criticism and book reviews
  • Political writing
  • Formal speeches and essays

You would not typically use it in casual everyday conversation — it would sound oddly grand. But in writing, or in any context where a significant departure is being discussed with appropriate gravity, it is exactly the right word.
The One-Line Summary to Remember It By
Valedictory describes something that formally and meaningfully says goodbye — it belongs to the moment of departure, not just the sequence of endings.
15459: A valedictory is a farewell speech — but not just any goodbye. It is a formal, carefully prepared address delivered at an important occasion to mark the end of a significant chapter in people's lives. Think of it as the official, meaningful "last word" before a group of people move on from something they shared together.
Where You'll Most Commonly Encounter It

The word is most strongly associated with graduation ceremonies. When a school or university class graduates, one student — typically the one with the highest academic rank, called the valedictorian — stands up and speaks on behalf of the entire graduating class. That speech is the valedictory.

It is the speech that says: "We did this together. Here's what it meant. Now we go forward."

A valedictory typically does three things at once:

  1. Looks back — It reflects on the shared journey. The struggles, the growth, the memories, the people who helped along the way.
  2. Acknowledges the present moment — It marks the significance of this exact turning point, the moment of departure.
  3. Looks forward — It sends people off with encouragement, hope, or a call to go out and do something meaningful with what they've learned.

This is why a valedictory tends to feel both celebratory and bittersweet at the same time. There's joy in the achievement, but there's also the quiet ache of leaving something behind.

While graduation is the most common setting, the word can be used more broadly for any formal farewell address that carries real weight. For example:

  • A long-serving president's final speech to the nation before leaving office can be called a valedictory.
  • A retiring judge's last address to a courtroom can be a valedictory.
  • A diplomat's final statement before leaving a post can be a valedictory.
  • A celebrated writer's final published essay, if it reads like a farewell, might be called a valedictory in literary contexts.

The key in all these cases is the same: it is formal, it is final, and it carries a sense of meaningful closure.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Valedictory" is not a cold or bureaucratic word. It carries genuine emotional depth. When someone calls a speech a valedictory, they're signalling that this isn't just a routine announcement — it is a deliberate, dignified farewell that deserves to be listened to carefully. It implies that what is ending actually mattered.
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "The class president gave a heartfelt valedictory that left many in the audience in tears."
  • "The retiring general's valedictory was broadcast on national television."
  • "After forty years in the Senate, her valedictory was considered one of the most eloquent speeches the chamber had ever heard."
  • "His valedictory focused entirely on the friendships that had carried the class through four difficult years."
One Simple Way to Remember It

If you ever forget the word's meaning, anchor it to this image: a student standing at a podium, facing their graduating class for the last time, about to say goodbye on everyone's behalf. That speech — that solemn, hopeful, final address — is a valedictory. Everything else the word means flows naturally from that image.
